title: Inside a CA
summary: What makes a certificate a CA, how deep a CA may go (pathlen), what each key may sign, and how to read what openssl verify says.

text: One extension makes a certificate a CA: basicConstraints. CA:TRUE, it may sign other certificates. CA:FALSE, it may not, whoever holds its key.
- A CA marks it critical: a client that doesn't understand it must refuse the certificate.
- Clients check it at each step of the chain: a server's certificate that signed another is refused (invalid CA certificate).

scheme: pathlen = how many CAs may come below
text: pathlen limits the depth below a CA. It keeps a CA you trust from making CAs of its own, out of your sight.
- pathlen:0: it signs servers' certificates only.
- Server certificates don't count, only the CAs between.
- On a Mac's LibreSSL: -text, and read Basic Constraints.

scheme: cRLSign            a CA: signs revocation lists
digitalSignature   a server: signs its TLS part
clientAuth         a client that logs in
text: keyUsage says what the key may sign. A CA needs keyCertSign, and cRLSign for its revocation lists. A server needs digitalSignature.
- extendedKeyUsage narrows it further: serverAuth for a web server.
- A CA whose keyUsage lacks keyCertSign gets what it signed refused: key usage does not include certificate signing.

scheme: error 25 at 2 depth lookup: path  ◀ why
text: openssl verify builds the chain like a client and says what breaks: the line above the error names the certificate, and the depth counts from the leaf (0).
- -untrusted gives the intermediates, -CAfile the root you trust. verify goes on after an error: read the first one.
- -verify_depth N refuses more than N intermediates (OpenSSL 3; a Mac's LibreSSL doesn't have it).
